opus-5.5.text:
I think language is underrated as a reason these models work so well. We often credit the architecture, the Transformer, or scaling, and those matter. But the data itself is very special.

Language is something humans have refined for thousands of years to compress our experience of the world. When we write, we've already done a huge amount of abstraction. We don't describe every pixel of a scene; we say "a cat sitting on a mat." So text is a highly distilled representation of reality, with most of the noise and redundancy stripped out. When a model learns from language, it's learning from data that has already been through human cognition. In a sense, it's standing on the shoulders of everyone who ever wrote anything down.

From a physics perspective, I like to think in terms of signal-to-noise and structure. Natural images or raw sensor data are high-dimensional, and the meaningful structure is buried in a lot of low-level detail. Language is low-dimensional in a useful way. It's discrete, it's compositional, and it has clear hierarchical structure: characters form words, words form phrases, phrases form arguments. That compositionality is exactly what next-token prediction can exploit. Predicting the next word forces the model to pick up grammar, then semantics, then some reasoning, because reasoning helps reduce prediction error.

This also explains why progress in vision and robotics has been slower. Those domains don't have a pre-compressed, human-curated representation. The model has to discover the abstractions itself, which is much harder.

But it also hints at a limitation. If language is a compression of the world made by humans, then a model trained only on language inherits both the strengths and the blind spots of that compression. Some things are hard to put into words: physical intuition, spatial reasoning, tacit skills. So I see language as the shortcut that let us get remarkably far very quickly. The open question is what it takes to go beyond it, whether models can build their own abstractions from raw experience the way humans originally did before we had language.

r002.rationale: It says language is an underrated reason these models work well and contrasts language’s contribution with architecture, which it says matters but is not the primary explanation.

r003.rationale: It describes language as compressed, compositional, and useful for next-token prediction, but does not say this makes architecture design comparatively less delicate.

fable-5.1.text:
I think language is doing something quite special, and it's easy to underestimate it. When people talk about why large language models work, they usually point to scale: more data, more parameters, more compute. All of that matters. But if you had the same scale and trained on, say, raw sensor streams or pixels alone, I don't think you'd get anything resembling the kind of reasoning we see today. Language is the thing that makes the whole recipe work.

The way I see it, language is a compressed record of human thought. Every sentence a person writes is already the output of a lot of cognitive work. Someone observed the world, abstracted it, picked out what mattered, and encoded it in symbols. So when a model trains on text, it's not learning from the world directly, it's learning from humanity's distilled interpretation of the world. It's like studying from the answer key rather than from raw experiment. That's an enormous head start.

Coming from physics, I tend to think about this in terms of representations. A good representation makes hard problems easy. Newton's laws look simple in the right coordinates and terrible in the wrong ones. Language, in a sense, is the coordinate system humans spent tens of thousands of years refining. Concepts like "cause," "because," "if," "more than," these are all abstractions that took us a long time to invent, and they're baked into the grammar for free. A model doesn't have to rediscover causality from scratch. The structure is sitting right there in the data.

There's also the point that language is discrete and compositional. You can take a finite set of tokens and combine them to express essentially infinite meanings. That compositionality is exactly what you want if you're hoping a system will generalize rather than just memorize. And next-token prediction, which sounds almost trivially simple, turns out to be a very demanding objective precisely because of this. To predict the next word well in a mathematical proof or a piece of code, you have to actually model the underlying logic. The objective is simple, but the data forces depth.

That said, I'd add one caveat. Language is a great teacher, but it's also a ceiling in some ways. The model inherits our abstractions, including our blind spots. If humans never put something into words, the model has a hard time getting it. So I think of language as the reason this first wave worked so well, and also as one of the things we'll eventually need to go beyond if we want models that discover genuinely new structure in the world rather than reorganizing what we already knew.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes language and scale but does not characterize LLMs as running counter to the Bitter Lesson.

r002.rationale: It says language makes the recipe work, but contrasts language with scale rather than with model architecture.

r003.rationale: It describes language as a compressed representation, but does not connect that structure to architecture design being comparatively less delicate.

astra-6.text:
I think language plays two roles here. First, it’s a medium for communication. But more importantly for large language models, it’s a medium in which humans have accumulated knowledge and organized thought. A piece of text contains more than facts—it can contain explanations, abstractions, and the steps of an argument.

So predicting the next word can be a much richer task than it sounds. To predict an explanation well across many different contexts, a model benefits from learning some of the relationships behind that explanation. The training objective is simple, but the structure in the data is not.

Language also gives us a shared interface across domains. We can describe a physics problem, a computer program, or an everyday decision in language. That lets one model learn across tasks that previously might have required separate systems.

But I wouldn’t equate language with intelligence itself. A lot of our understanding comes from perception and interaction with the world, and text only captures part of that. I see language as an extraordinarily powerful starting point: it gives models access to the knowledge humans have made explicit, while leaving open the question of what they still need to learn through experience.

r001.rationale: The response does not characterize large language models as running counter to the Bitter Lesson.

r002.rationale: It describes language as useful for learning knowledge and tasks, but does not say language itself is the primary cause of LLM success relative to model architecture.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss architecture design or claim that language’s compressed structure makes it less delicate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language plays two roles. First, it’s a medium for accumulating knowledge. When we train a model on text, we’re giving it access to traces of how people describe the world, solve problems, and communicate ideas. So the model isn’t learning only grammar; it’s also learning some of the structure behind those descriptions.

Second, language gives us a shared interface for many different tasks. You can ask a question, describe a goal, provide an example, or explain a mistake—all through the same medium. That makes it possible for one model to learn across tasks that previously would have required separate systems.

But I would distinguish language from the world itself. Text contains a lot of information about physical reality, but it leaves things out. We don’t write down every detail of how we move, perceive, or interact with objects. So language is an incredibly powerful starting point for intelligence, but whether it is sufficient depends on what kinds of intelligence we want the model to develop.
